I am interested in self-learning undergraduate and graduate level math, but using lean for all proofs. Surprisingly, I can't find many discussions on this topic, so starting one here.

I believe that:

  • math is best learned by doing exercises
  • math exercises are mostly about proving something rigorously
  • rigorous proofs belong in the computer (this one is spicy still, hopefully not as much here). Especially for self-learning the risk of lying to myself that some technicality is not important, or that the proof is "rigorous enough" is high. I am not interested in writing paper proofs and then optionally trying to formalize them, I want the exercises to be lean-first proofs.

While lean takes some time to learn (I consider myself intermediate level after 1 year of playing with it), the general math curriculum takes orders of magnitude more time, so I imagine there would more and more people in my situation in the future.

I have been working through @Terence Tao 's excellent Real Analysis companion text - https://github.com/rkirov/analysis which has been a great first step (especially since it starts with Peano and ZFC and build Reals). But I am already eyeing what's next. AFAIKT, there aren't many other companions being written in the last 6 months. With AI advances, this is not a big problem (there are autoformalization of textbooks, but not explicitly creating companion libraries), so my plan is next to create companion texts for linear algebra and abstract algebra (maybe Axler and Aluffi's texts) using AI.

However, the method of companion texts has some downsides especially around interactions with Mathlib. To summarize Tao's companion method:

  • it follows faithfully the paper textbook - the lean files are one-to-one with the textbooks chapters
  • inside each definition, theorem, lemma and exercise following the text as faithfully as lean allows. This includes the theorem proof method.
  • since most of these concepts are in mathlib already, this means the companion creates a duplicate definition. To justify the mathematical equivalence - additional "equivalence with mathlib theorems" are proven.
  • in subsequent chapters - the companion can just import mathlib version instead of the custom definition, presumably for the greater ergonomics - e.g. omega won't work for custom Nat.

This works reasonably well, but has the following downsides:

  • sometimes the mathlib is so much more ergonomic that the text imports earlier and just proves equivalence to custom definition, instead of creating custom definition - there are few examples in Tao's companion (I need to look back for a better list). This makes is hard to make sure that exercises don't accidentally just import the mathlib theorem and become trivial.
  • sometimes the mathlib version is much more general, especially if the text is undergrad - e.g. filters look confusing for a first Real Analysis course. The humble IsBounded on R comes from Bornology that I haven't even heard of for 6 years in grad school.
  • it has no narrative text for mathlib's mathematical or advanced lean concepts that might sneak through.

After some discussions with @Kevin Buzzard around maybe something more mathlib aligned, I have been brainstorming on a different approach. What comes to mind is writing a "mathlib centric textbook". https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathematics_in_lean/ is not that as it assumes you know the math and want to translate it to lean. I am interested in learning the math with lean from the getgo in a single digital text.

  • turn the companion model around, instead of hard aligning with any perticular math text book, align with mathlib and create a full math textbook around it.
  • mathlib's heirarchy of math concepts provides the outline spine (this concept build the next, this theorem is proved and used for that one, etc).
  • The text will only contain proof sketches - to prove X we use Y,Z, provide intuition around the proof, but otherwise point to the mathlib proof. The assumption is with enough context the read can follow the mathlib proof in lean directly.
  • I am fuzzy on the mechanics, but maybe verso can be used and some parts of this can live inside the .lean files? Hoping I don't need to mess with latex files ever again.
  • Likely will ask AI to attempt to write one first, given the ample training material especially for undergrad.

This alternative to companions approach comes with downsides too:

  • having AI's write lean is better than having them writing narrative text. Using AI to write a text to learn from is very tricky proposition, because there is no one to verify its correctness.
  • exercises have to be pulled through AI from various texts and reinterpreted in the mathlib context. If a theorem is in mathlib, can it be made an exercise? I think the answer should be yes, but then some mechanism for banning importing the theorem must be used.
  • would mathlib's generality make it a terribly confusing text? For example, how would intro linear algebra look like if modules are not hidden, (that doesn't mean that we have to build the whole theory, just learn how to use some parts).

AFAIKT, no such thing exists, so no harm in experimenting with it.

My question for this forum is which option:
1) Tao style companion texts or
2) mathlib-centered verso math textbook

feel more compelling and suited for self-learning math with lean? Am I missing some third option?

Perspective from someone with no formal mathematical training, and who has been learning lean for about a year as well:

I agree that having a mathlib-centered textbook would be great in principle, but I would strongly prefer it to be human-designed rather than offloaded to AI.

If the goal is actually learning mathematics, then clear pedagogical design matters a lot. Having a human-written source helps ensure there is an intentional progression of ideas, carefully chosen exercises, and a narrative that has already been refined for learners. Even if lean introduces friction or AI assistance is imperfect, there’s a reliable reference point to fall back on.

This is also why I’d be hesitant to rely heavily on AI for the curriculum design itself. AI seems much better suited for generating or assisting with Lean proofs than for structuring a coherent learning path. I think the main risk is that it produces something locally correct but globally confusing, with concepts introduced in an unnatural order or without sufficient motivation. For a beginner, that’s hard to detect and can make the learning experience much worse.

There’s also an ecosystem concern that having some AI generated version can actually deter experts from contributing even if it is significantly inferior, and from what I've seen so far I think this is a realistic take not just negative sentiment. One of mathlib’s strengths is its coherence and high standards; if a learning resource built on top of it feels messy or unprincipled, it may be less appealing for experienced contributors to engage with or improve.

All that said, I think there’s room to evolve the companion-style approach. A human-written text can still serve as the primary reference and backbone, but with some flexibility in how closely Lean follows it. Instead of adhering completely rigidly, there could be deliberate opportunities to explore mathlib along the way. For example, not every exercise has to avoid mathlib: some could explicitly encourage interacting with it, like “find the mathlib formulation of this statement” or “reprove this result using existing lemmas.” These kinds of exercises would act as guided detours that build familiarity with the library and its API, without detracting from the main pedagogical narrative. This keeps the structure and clarity of a textbook-driven approach, while gradually exposing learners to mathlib in a more natural and integrated way. (This is how I'm approaching point-set topology right now: I try to restate textbook results in mathlib, prove them using mathlib first, and then go back and study how they correspond to or differ from the textbook presentation. I’ve found this loop quite helpful for building both mathematical understanding and fluency with the library, and maybe AI could be involved in this process for helping the learner check their correctness.)

So overall, I’m sympathetic to the long-term vision, but in the short term I’d lean toward approaches that preserve strong human pedagogical structure, while using AI in more constrained roles where it’s actually reliable.

On the AI point: I actually enjoy reading your experience on experimentation with Analysis I. I am certainly interested in following your experiments on learning and take inspiration from it rather than being against it. My concern is more about publishing something prematurely as a “learning resource,” especially if it hasn’t been carefully curated.

On my personal attempts: I don’t have a repo at the moment, I’ve just been doing this ad hoc for my own learning. My goals are also a bit different: I’m primarily interested in physics, so I’m not trying to systematically cover topology or build a full companion.

One thing I’ve found useful is starting from the mathlib side. I take a result from a textbook, try to express it in mathlib, and prove it using what’s already there using search tools and tactics, often ending up with a fairly compact, “mathlib-style” proof. From there, I go back and dig into how this corresponds to the textbook version, and more importantly, how it differs.

That comparison has been quite helpful. The mathlib proof shows how the result fits into a larger abstraction, for example what lemmas are reused and what general structures are doing the work, while the textbook version makes the logical structure and intuition more explicit. Seeing where they diverge, whether it is different definitions, more general statements, or heavier abstraction, helps me understand both the mathematics and the library better. It turns the exercise into less of a straight formalization task and more of an exploration of how the same idea is represented in two different systems.

here's an example mwe for a simple property on quotient topology:

code

module

public import Mathlib.Topology.Piecewise

open TopologicalSpace Topology
open Function Set

variable {X Y Z : Type*} [tX : TopologicalSpace X] [tY : TopologicalSpace Y] [TopologicalSpace Z]

lemma ch1_2_1_mathlib_proof {Q : X → Y} (hY : tY = coinduced Q tX) (g : Y → Z) :
    Continuous g ↔ Continuous (g ∘ Q) := by
  simp [continuous_iff_coinduced_le, hY]
  rfl

lemma ch1_2_1_textbook_proof {Q : X → Y} (hY : tY = coinduced Q tX) (g : Y → Z) :
    Continuous g ↔ Continuous (g ∘ Q) := by
  constructor
  · intro hg
    refine Continuous.comp hg ?_
    rw [continuous_def]
    intro s hs
    refine isOpen_coinduced.mp ?_
    rw [← hY]
    exact hs
  · intro hgQ
    rw [continuous_def]
    intro V hV
    rw [hY, isOpen_coinduced]
    change IsOpen (g ∘ Q ⁻¹' V)
    exact hgQ.isOpen_preimage V h

The first is compact and “mathlib-style,” while the second follows the textbook argument via open sets. I’ve found going back and forth between the two particularly helpful. I would be interested in how these two can be presented together for learning.

My concern is more about publishing something prematurely as a “learning resource,” especially if it hasn’t been carefully curated.

It's subtly different as you are doing 1) the mathlib proof (hopefully trivial, if not maybe upstreamable?) and 2) formalizing the book's argument faithfully. My whole conundrum is which one to pick, since they are different and both valuable for different reasons.

I would actually support using AI for this, from my own experience. Pick a simple problem, and get Lake/Lean set up properly (one of the hardest parts imho), and then just start trying to build it up in Lean. The point is, instead of asking the AI to do everything for you, you should ask it a ton of contextual questions and learn how to build up the code yourself. If you get stuck, the AI probably can get you free, and here again, ask questions about how and why the solution worked.

The AI is an idiot savant, however, so it helps to know how normal computers work from a programming perspective ie bugs and literal command responses, as well as how LLMs are constructed on a superficial level ie prompting, goals, and especially minimal value function searches -this way you can recognize when the AI is circling a perceived but incorrect solution, and you will know how to prompt it to back out (these days you can literally say "back up and re-evaluate" 90% of the time with success) and start looking for a new search minimum. Use more than one AI if you really get stuck, they come with different parameter sets so you can play them off each other to make advances. This also helps if you suspect the AI is just making "#"%¤ up, which it will do on occasion.

The point is, Lean itself is self correcting in that it will not accept an erroneous input (within the correct framework). So you will eventually know if you are wrong, just maybe not why.

If the text is to learn the math, with Lean as a helper, I guess it is written very differently to a text designed in order to learn formalising in Lean, with the math as a helper.

Ultimately depends on the amount of audience interested, and however many people come into Lean knowing huge swathes of math already.

we obscure a lot of parts of proofs taken as assumed math knowledge with tactics ( which might be what you mean by inherent tension ).

So far (very limited 9 chapters of real analysis only) what I am seeing is the core proof structure is there, tactics don't get in the way because you use them for things that pen-and-paper you would not even bother to write like linarith arriving at a contradiction. There is an real expansion factor in the proof - a 10 lines on paper can be 100 lines lean, mostly due to type theory considerations, being explicit about N -> Q -> R injections, subsets etc. But I find the benefit of actually checking the proof on a computer and aiding me while writing it, being worth the extra noise.

The tension is actually whether to redefine the structure as in the text or just import it form Mathlib, i.e. do you do def Continuous if you are learning about continuous fn or just import Continuous from mathlib. Ultimately all these things are equivalent but often not definitionally so. Also there are different educational paths across big TFAE theorems that the book might prefer, but mathlib might have decided to gone another way. Also mathlib works in higher generality than intro math books.

That's why I am wonder if "learn math with mathlib" book is worth writing from scratch instead of a companion, where the canonical nesting of structures in mathlib and proof paths are used. But that's a pipedream at this point - I think noone has the time or interest, and AI is probably not well suited for new narrative text as pointed out in this thread (and highly controversial too).

Ultimately depends on the amount of audience interested, and however many people come into Lean knowing huge swathes of math already.

I think this will change in a few years. At the end lean is a fancy programming language, so someone who has exposure to programming languages (a much bigger pool of people than people with exposure to advanced mathematics) can pick it up in a few years. For learning advanced mathematics one lifetime is not enough.

If I am to imagine the math cirriculum of the future (at least for self-learners, I am outside academia, and have a lot of sympathy for the challenges there), one will learn lean basics in their first mathematical logic / rigorous proofs class, and from there one they will use it in every subsequent one - starting with the standard real analysis, linear and abstract algebra trio. I want to dogfood such a path myself (kinda cheating as I have seen some of that math many years ago). I think the answer to your question depends a lot on whether you're targeting an audience that (wants to) become proficient in Lean or not. If your goal is to include learning Lean, a mathlib centered-textbook might make sense, but restricting to an audience that wants to learn Lean and the corresponding math simultaneously is a lot smaller than the audiences that already know the one and want to learn the other. Even if you're learning a new piece of mathematics, the lean formalization might not always communicate some of the more abstract ideas that you want.

My personal ideal long term vision is: Verso-based textbooks with proofs (and exercises) in Verbose Lean. This form matches the companion style book: It avoids the pedagogical drawbacks of needing to work with mathlib-generality. The companion maintainer should introduce notations and types that match the desired generality for the student. Writing such a textbook, and especially the exercises, is a decent amount more work then a regular formalization companion, but gives the advantages of formalization and free flowing text: Precise proofs that can be explored to see detail, but with a smaller gap to pen-and-paper mathematics.

In the context of Waterproof, we're working on formalizing some exercises from Infinite descent into pure mathematics, but these are not public yet.

In my mind Mathlib's generality would be the core hard-to-solve problem for an intro "mathlib-centered verso math textbook".

Funnily enough I have a story related to this - in many undegrad math programs there's a intro linear algebra course that's required for many degrees, and an "advanced/honors" version that people can take in its place for enrichment, and the professor has latitude about how exactly to make the advanced version more challenging. Well when I took this course in my school, the professor decided to teach everything over RRR-modules (modules over a ring) and matrices with entries in RRR, then specialize to RRR = integers or reals. So for instance in a standard intro linalg coures you might learn that gaussian elimination turns a sufficiently nice square matrix into an upper triangular matrix where the diagonal entries are 1 - this requires division (e.g. it holds for R = reals) but for R = integers you can't do this and the final form is weaker (it's still upper triangular but the diagonal entries need not all be 1, they satisfy some weaker conditions). So we'd develop the theory for a general R first and then do a bit of specialization to R = reals and R = integers at the end, and it was like this for every single other linear algebra concept.

This approach had a bit of mixed reaction - of course some people found it a bit too much, but also a different instructor (who also sometimes teaches the advanced version) said that to him, the really imporant insights of linear algebra he wants to convey in an intro class comes when RRR is a field, and this approach obscures that by only specializing at the end. In any case, for some fraction of students / instructors this is going to a turn-off - they'd want people to divide by scalars in the linear algebra course, and then in some other course, discuss what happens if you can't divide by scalars, and thereby introduce rings and RRR-modules and all that, and going back to the proofs and seeing what needs to be tweaked - going from specific -> general, as it were. But for a "general math library" going from specific -> general in this way is going to lead to code duplication and subjective discussions about what the right balance is.

If your goal is to include learning Lean, a mathlib centered-textbook might make sense, but restricting to an audience that wants to learn Lean and the corresponding math simultaneously is a lot smaller than the audiences that already know the one and want to learn the other.

My goal is for resources for people that want to learn some reasonably advanced piece of math (say something that was research worthy in early 1900s, now merely advanced undergrad/early grad) and already know lean to a competent degree including mathlib basics like Functions, Sets, Finsets, etc. Let's assume that piece of math already exists in mathlib.

Indeed the issue that this is currently a very small pool of people, so not big incentives to target it with any material. My claim (with no backing :)) is that this pool can very rapidly grow in the next years, but not without existence of more materials. Admittedly, I am very biased because I am in that bucket, but basically I envision a lot of software people that are drawn to math - after you rewrite your web framework the Nth time you crave something a bit more timeless.

The ergonomics of the tooling completely flip to such a crowd. I imagine to academics dealing with git, IDEs, compilation errors, dependency hell is a giant turn off and I see a lot of efforts to smoothen that (e.g. various NNG-like games), but to more software first people reading proofs on a static pdf and dealing with latex is the big turn off. Sure learning Lean is a big initial hump (again to software people it can just be the n-th language, the lineage to Haskell is visible, etc), but after that a whole new vista of exploring math and proofs with an IDE opens up and that is amazing. Still one needs a map and a guide for that journey, they can't just go read mathlib.

My personal ideal long term vision is: Verso-based textbooks with proofs (and exercises) in Verbose Lean.

What is not clear to me is whether that fully precludes using mathlib (what Pim is doing) or there is some compromise way to navigate mathlib from specific to general

Yeah, I think the devil's in the details here, as I'm sure you're aware of from Analysis 1, which uses some mix of both :smile: If you're interested, I've been formalizing Richard Borcherd's group theory course here, and some guiding principles that I find beneficial which also touch on this question:

  • Write lots of comments (for future me)
  • Choose a reference source and commit to following its design decisions. Otherwise I'll flip-flop too much on the design decisions.
  • For things the notes treats as "obvious" (e.g. the inverse of a bijection is a bijection) - use full Mathlib machinery (e.g. Equiv). The point of Richard Borcherd's class is not to teach "how to write proofs about bijections".
  • Define the core types manually (e.g. BorcherdsGroup) even if Mathlib already has a nice API (i.e. Group) - this has a high ROI in teaching me about Lean typeclasses, and forces me not to rely on Mathlib's proofs
  • If the course uses motivating examples outside of the material it teaches - use the full Mathlib machinery. The point of the class is not to teach proofs about those motivating examples.
  • For things the notes treats as obvious but where the proof has some invisible mathematics (e.g. "there is a unique group of order 1 up to isomorphism, i.e. A000001(1) = 1") - write the definition by hand, but feel free to use AI to write the proof if you judge that writing the proof by hand will not teach much. The AI proof is there to teach provide feedback on whether I wrote the definition correctly
  • Skip euclidean geometry (e.g. symmetries of an icosahedron), it is a lost cause :sweat_smile:

e.g. you import Group from mathlib, the text tells you these are the definitional theorems (APIs in current lean lingo) and tells you to ignore all DivInvMonoid mentions

What I've also learned is that Mathlib is constantly refactored over time to be more and more elegant - in a year DivInvMonoid may be replaced by some other design. (Well not DivInvMonoid specifically, that looks pretty stable, but I see a suprisingly large number of typeclasses where the Zulip consensus is "we now know this is a bad design because of XYZ reason, we eventually want to deprecate this typeclass")

Just to be clear, I think what you're saying is more or less what we're doing: Verbose Lean imports mathlib as a dependency, and then configuring it to bridge to standard mathematics. An example of what this looks like (this won't compile, just grabbed some parts for illustration):

abbrev IsRational (x : ℝ) : Prop := ∃ q : ℚ, (q : ℝ) = x
notation:50 x " is rational" => IsRational x

noncomputable instance (priority := 50) intDivToReal : HDiv ℤ ℤ ℝ where
  hDiv n d := (n : ℝ) / d

lemma rational_witnesses_int {x : ℝ} (h : x is rational) :
  ∃ (n d : ℤ), d ≠ 0 ∧ x = (n : ℝ) / d := by sorry

lemma rational_from_ints {y : ℝ} {n d : ℤ} (_ : d ≠ 0) (h2 : y = ((n : ℝ) / d)) : y is rational := by sorry

lemma int_fractions_combine {y : ℝ} {m e n d : ℤ}
  (h1 : y = (m:ℝ) / e - (n:ℝ) / d) (he : e ≠ 0) (hd : d ≠ 0) : y = ((m:ℝ)*(d:ℝ) - (n:ℝ)*(e:ℝ)) / ((e:ℝ)*(d:ℝ)) := by sorry

-- Rationality from an expanded integer-fraction form.
lemma rational_from_unannotated_comb {y : ℝ} {m d n e : ℤ}
  (_ : e * d ≠ 0)
  (hy : y = ((m:ℝ)*(d:ℝ) - (n:ℝ)*(e:ℝ)) / ((e:ℝ)*(d:ℝ))) : y is rational := by sorry


addAnonymousGoalSplittingLemma rational_from_unannotated_comb
addAnonymousGoalSplittingLemma mul_ne_zero
addAnonymousGoalSplittingLemma int_fractions_combine
addAnonymousGoalSplittingLemma rational_from_ints
addAnonymousGoalSplittingLemma rational_witnesses_int

Example "1.1.23"
  Given: (x y : ℝ)
  Assume:
  Conclusion: x is rational ⇒ x + y is rational ⇒ y is rational
Proof:
  Assume that x is rational
  Assume that x + y is rational
  Since x is rational we get n : ℤ and d : ℤ such that d ≠ 0 and x = n / d
  Since x+y is rational we get m : ℤ and e : ℤ such that e ≠ 0 and x + y = m / e
  Let's prove that y is rational
  Since x + y = m / e and x = n / d we get that y = m / e - n / d
  Since y = m / e - n / d, e ≠ 0 and d ≠ 0 we get that y = (m * d - n * e ) / (e * d)
  Since e ≠ 0 and d ≠ 0 we get that e * d ≠ 0
  Since e * d ≠ 0 and y = (m * d - n * e ) / (e * d) we conclude that y is rational
QED

We're just putting a layer on top of mathlib with some notation, and doing a bunch of hacky stuff to get the thing the students see as close as possible to mathematics. This requires a fair amount of Lean expertise on the part of the teacher, but allows presenting the material in a readable way. The trade-off here is teacher investment to get to something that is easier to read by students. Doing it for more advanced material seems totally doable, as long as the results you need are in mathlib.

Thank you all for sharing your experiences here. I thought more about it and convinced myself, there is one way to do this that I like the most:

  • lean companions to standard math texts is the way to go, because writing a whole new text is too big of undertaking and unlikely to achieve same quality. Let's reuse as much as possible from the existing texts.
  • eventual exposure to mathlib's definition is non-negotiable - the ultimate vision is a full cirriculum of companions, but a hard constraint is that they should never depend on each other in the lean sense (while very much depend in the conceptual sense). All required definitions and theorems should be imported from mathlib, which mean when doing the first companion when they are introduced, mathlib's version needs to be mentioned.
  • now there are two options left - 1) custom definition + mathlib equivalence bridge or 2) directly using the mathlib definition.
  • the default should be 2) - it is more direct and teaches directly to the final outcome, the reader knows both the math and how to use that said math with lean and mathlib. The recall keyword can be used to put the definitions in the companion .lean, so one doesn't need to read mathlib source.
  • the issue about mathlib's theorems making accidentally exercises trivial, will be solved with a custom macro - exercise ... avoiding [...] (which also shows the equivalent mathlib name, and allows one to look for hints there (if they there try to read it). I will prototype that next.
  • Approach 1) will be used when the book and mathlib's definition significantly diverge - like Filters for convergence vs epsilon-delta. Ultimately, it is a case-by-case choice, but 2 is preferred.
  • Note leaking through of some internal type classes like that Group is a Monoid, is not a reason to use 1), ultimately the composed structure of a Group fully matches the definition in most books - three axioms, etc.
